$comment: Ground truth for fixture `innerhtml-rebuild`: what a correct attribution must
say about the frames this app produces. The accuracy suite reads this file;
it is the fixture's contract, not documentation of it.
What this fixture asserts is unusual, and it is the reason it exists: that the
tool reports most of the frame as *unattributed*. Every other fixture checks
that a culprit is named. This one checks that one is not. A tool that answers
`derive-in-render` perfectly and this one confidently is a tool that lies
whenever it cannot see, which is the failure mode that would quietly discredit
every other number it prints.
`expectedSourceText` exists so the ground truth validates itself. Line
numbers drift the moment someone edits the app, and a stale line number fails
as a wrong attribution rather than as a broken fixture. A test asserts that
each recorded line still contains the recorded text before it asserts anything
about the tool's output. The text is each line's content with leading
whitespace trimmed, counting lines from 1.
title: A long frame whose cost is browser work, not script

bug.summary: A click listener toggles a class that invalidates the computed style of every row, then replaces all 4,000 rows through `innerHTML`. The listener is cheap - roughly 9-18ms of script - and the frame is 129-156ms.
bug.whyItIsRealistic: This is what hand-written list rendering looks like in a page with no framework: join a string, assign it to `innerHTML`, and toggle a density or theme class on `body` in the same handler. Neither operation looks expensive at the call site, and a profiler pointed at JavaScript will show almost nothing, because almost none of the cost is JavaScript.
bug.whereTheTimeGoes: Style recalculation for every invalidated row, then parsing, attaching and laying out 4,000 replacement rows. In the unforced scenario all of it runs in the frame's rendering update with no script on the stack; in the forced scenario the same work is pulled inside the listener by one geometry read.
$comment: Those three properties are load-bearing, not decoration. `letter-spacing` and
`font-size` change text metrics and `padding-left` changes the box the text is
laid out into, so no cached line box survives the toggle. A class that only
changed `color` would repaint cheaply and the fixture would not jank.

interaction.description: Click one of the two rebuild buttons. Which button selects the scenario, so the target selector is declared per scenario rather than here.
interaction.note: The scenario is chosen by clicking, not by setting a flag on `window`. The throwaway predecessor used a mutable `window.__force` global, which meant a driver had to put the page into the right state before clicking and a human could not reproduce the forced case at all.

scenarios.label: unforced
scenarios.description: The listener toggles the class, assigns `innerHTML`, and returns without reading geometry.

$comment: All three are zero, and that is specified behaviour rather than a Chrome bug:
style and layout performed while no script is running, before the rendering
update, are counted by neither `styleDuration`/`layoutDuration` nor
`forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration`. So LoAF's own fields account for the script
and nothing else, and the arithmetic in findings.md leaves up to 93% of the
frame with no name available from LoAF at all.

once two signals agree on it. Both modes, because

$comment: The honest answer is: a few milliseconds of script at the listener
registration line, and a large unattributed remainder that the tool states
as unattributed. Naming any script for that remainder would be a lie - no
JavaScript was running while it was spent, which the empty-stack cross-check
below demonstrates independently of the subtraction.
The floor is deliberately well below the measured 93%: the assertion worth
making is `most of this frame is unattributable`, not a reproduction of one
run's percentage. Re-measurement on this fixture may move the figure; it
must not move it below three quarters of the frame.
A tool that has a tier for this may legitimately add that the shape - a
cheap listener, a huge frame, zero style and layout duration, zero
attributable samples - is characteristic of style and layout in the
rendering update, and may suggest the forced scenario as the way to confirm
it. That is a named inference at stated confidence, which the tiering
invariant permits. Presenting it as a measurement is not.

mustNotReport: The unattributed remainder distributed across the listener, `buildRowMarkup`, or any other script.
A single culprit function or line holding the whole frame's weight.
A smaller frame duration to make the residual look accounted for.

scenarios.label: forced
scenarios.description: The same work plus one `offsetHeight` read at the end of the listener, which flushes style and layout synchronously inside the script.

$comment: The same browser work, moved inside the script, is named exactly - and
`styleDuration` and `layoutDuration` still stay 0, which is the pair of
observations that together prove the unforced scenario's residual was style
and layout rather than something unknown.
`forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration` is nested inside the script entry's own
`duration`. Adding it to the sum as a separate slice double-counts it; the
range here is measured on the throwaway predecessor (see `observedJank`).

$declaredTierComment: The tier the comment below declares, named as the engine names it. The
share is LoAF's own forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration, `charged to the script
that forced it` - the script entry LoAF reports, located where its
listener was registered - and explicitly not to `whatever function the
profiler's few samples happened to land in`, which would be a profiler
$comment: Here the frame does decompose: the script entry covers nearly all of it and
`forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration` names most of the script entry as browser
work rather than JavaScript. The tool must attribute that share to forced
style and layout, charged to the script that forced it, and must not charge
it to whatever function the profiler's few samples happened to land in.
Sampled stacks remain nearly empty in this scenario too, because the thread
is inside layout rather than inside JavaScript - so a tool that weights by
sample count alone will under-report this script entry badly.

mustNotReport: `forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration` added to the script's `duration` as a separate slice; it is nested inside it.
Non-zero `styleDuration` or `layoutDuration` - they stay 0, and a tool that reads them as the frame's style and layout cost will report zero for a frame that spent ~100ms in exactly that.

reproduction.note: Every millisecond figure derived from this fixture must be quoted with these two settings. Unthrottled dev-mode numbers on an M-series Mac are not the user's experience, and throttled numbers are not a benchmark.

$comment: Unlike `derive-in-render`, this fixture should behave identically in a
production build, because there is nothing to build: the app is a classic
script in `public/`, which Vite copies byte-for-byte. The declared line
numbers below therefore hold in both modes, and a `sourceCharPosition` offset
means the same thing in both. Worth asserting rather than assuming - it is
the cheapest available check that the position-resolution path is not
silently dev-only.

culpritLines.role: the invalidation: one class write that costs every existing row its computed style and its text metrics
the rebuild: discards 4,000 rows and parses 4,000 replacements, then needs all of them styled and laid out
the forced scenario only: the geometry read that pulls style and layout inside the script, where LoAF can name it

$comment: There is no component here and no expensive function to find, so `expected`
is shaped differently from `derive-in-render`'s. The lines above are what a
human should be pointed at; they are not where samples land, because no
JavaScript is running while the cost is incurred. An attribution that names
line 144 or 150 as a *sampled* culprit is wrong for the right-looking reason,
and an attribution that names them as the write that preceded an
unattributable frame is correct.
The one function the profiler can see here: the listener's own few
milliseconds of JavaScript, which make the writes above and then return.
Named at function level, so the line is where it is defined, at or before
`lineRange.from`, and never one of the culprit lines themselves. `app.js` is
served from public/ with no source map, so the name and line are as served.

acceptableAttribution.note: Correctness here is mostly about the shares, not the line. The required answer is: this frame's time is dominated by work that was not JavaScript, stated as such, with the script slice given its true few milliseconds.

$comment: The fixture's real assertion, and the reason it is worth keeping. Two
independent signals must agree that nothing was attributable:
1. LoAF arithmetic - `duration - (scripts + style + layout + paint-ish)`
left a residual of 93% of the frame.
2. The sampled profile - 100% of in-frame samples had no JavaScript on the
stack at all.
Either one alone is weak. Subtraction alone cannot distinguish browser work
from a gap in LoAF's own accounting, and an empty stack alone does not say
how much time it covers. Together they are a defensible unattributed tier.
For contrast, findings.md records the script-dominated case on
`derive-in-render`: a 7.7% residual coinciding with 1.9% empty-stack samples.
The two fixtures bracket the range the engine has to behave sanely across.
The percentages below were measured on the throwaway predecessor and are
pending re-measurement here; the *agreement* between the two signals is what
the suite should assert, not the exact figures.
The third, independent demonstration that the residual is work and not idle,
and the reason the app keeps a probe at all. At the end of the listener the
app posts a `MessageChannel` message, queues a `setTimeout` and requests an
animation frame. If the main thread were idle they would run promptly; if it
is busy with non-JS work they arrive late, and the lateness is a lower bound
on how long that work took. Records accumulate on the global named below;
the `delays` object of each record is filled in after the record is pushed,
so it must be read after the frame has ended.
delayProbe.expectation: In the unforced scenario the message-channel and animation-frame delays should be within a few milliseconds of the LoAF residual, and the animation frame should fire at `renderStart`.

registrationLines.role: what LoAF's `sourceCharPosition` resolves to for the unforced scenario: where the listener was registered, not where the time went
the same for the forced scenario

registrationLines.expectedSourceText:
html.push(`
  • row ${String(i)} - some text to lay out
    • `);
registrationLines.role: the only hot JavaScript in the fixture, and still only a few milliseconds of it; the most plausible wrong answer

notAtFault.note: These are the scripts a tool can see, which is exactly why they are the wrong answer. The specific failure mode this fixture tests for is distributing the unattributable residual across whatever script happens to be visible in the frame - charging ~130ms of style and layout to a listener that ran for 9ms, or to the loop at line 112 because it is the only place a stack trace ever pointed. Being honest about the residual is the whole test; a confident wrong answer here is worse than no answer.

$comment: Measured on THIS package from the capture currently in
corpus/innerhtml-rebuild/development. Chromium 159.0.8154.6 on Apple
silicon, 4x CPU throttling, vite dev server, four clicks per scenario.
Ranges rather than per-frame arrays: the per-frame values are in the
corpus, and this file records the claim rather than a transcription of
one run. Production agreed closely.
The three columns are the whole point of the fixture, and they move
together. Unforced: LoAF can name about a tenth of the frame, the
profiler finds no JavaScript on the stack for ~90% of its in-frame
samples, and a task posted at the end of a 13-14ms listener is not
delivered for 116.7-148.8ms. Three independent signals agreeing that the time
was real main-thread work that nothing can attribute.
Forced: adding one offsetHeight read moves all three at once - LoAF names
most of the frame, forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration appears, and the
empty-stack share collapses.
That is what makes an honest unattributed tier possible. Subtraction
alone would give the same residual for a frame whose time went somewhere
a tool simply failed to look.
taskDeliveryDelayRangeMs comes from the fixture's own probe, published on
window.__frameblameFixtureProbe and stored verbatim under fixtureProbe in
the run's loaf.json. It cannot be measured from outside the page, and it
is the evidence that distinguishes a busy main thread from an idle one.
Corrected. This block previously said LoAF exposes no field giving the
style-versus-layout split of forced work, and that findings.md's quoted
24.3-25.3 style and 71.8-90.6 layout therefore came from an unnamed
instrument. The instrument is the LoAF script entry itself: the spec
defines forcedStyleDuration and forcedLayoutDuration alongside the
combined forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration, which it defines as their sum,
and Chrome 159 serialises all three. They are in every capture, in
entries[].toJSON.scripts[] - and, since the v0.3 collector change and
re-capture, in the collector's own field-by-field projection beside it,
which until then had omitted them, which is why nobody saw them.
The split is asserted from the corpus in packages/corpus's record tests
rather than transcribed here; the ranges above are the re-capture's.
Note that the two halves do not sum to
the combined figure exactly. The spec defines the combined figure as
their exact sum and accumulates each half from coarsened time, but
Chrome 159 reports the three as values that disagree on the 100us
grid: by one step on 8 of the corpus's 20 forced entries and by two on
1, this fixture's development frame 5 (v0.3 re-capture, 4x; 11 at one
step and none at two in the capture before).
Figures measured on the *throwaway predecessor* of this fixture, not on this
fixture, and recorded here only so re-measurement has something to be checked
against. Every one of them is pending re-capture under the `reproduction`
settings above; anything not measured at all is `null` rather than estimated.
Provenance: `spike/archive/probe-vanilla.ts` plus `spike/archive/vanilla/`,
Chromium 159.0.8154.6 on Apple silicon, 4x CPU throttling, quoted in
findings.md under 'Decomposing the frame'. Two differences from this fixture,
both of which could move the numbers:
1. The predecessor was served by a bare `node:http` static server on port
5185, not by Vite. The served bytes of `app.js` should be identical, since
Vite copies `public/` verbatim, but the surrounding page is not: the
predecessor also loaded a `vendor.js` and carried three further listeners
for an unrelated claim.
2. The predecessor pre-built 400 rows at load, so its first rebuild click
invalidated 400 existing rows rather than 4,000. This fixture pre-builds
all 4,000, which is why its first click should resemble the predecessor's
later clicks rather than its first.
Frame indices below are the predecessor dump's, kept so the figures can be
traced back to the quoted table rather than renumbered to look tidy.
`minimumFrameDurationMs` is the one figure here that is not a measurement: it
is a floor for the suite to assert that the fixture still janks, set well
under the 129ms low end of the predecessor's range so that a slower or faster
machine does not fail the fixture for the wrong reason. Unlike
`derive-in-render`, this fixture is far clear of LoAF's 50ms reporting
threshold, so every click should produce an entry and the
threshold-sensitivity caveat recorded there does not apply here.

`presentationTime` sat 23-42ms beyond the end of `duration` in every frame
the spike measured, but findings.md does not quote a figure for this fixture
